summary: Mobility is returning toward pre‑pandemic levels with an MF‑Index of 71, but public transport ridership remains about 14% below 2019 levels and actual fuel savings are far below the theoretical ceiling. High‑risk sectors such as retail, logistics and construction continue to show very high mobility scores, signalling exposure to congestion and emissions risks.

signals.detail: While the modelled ceiling suggests 35.7 M L/week could be saved, only 334 k L were actually saved in the first week of the mandate, representing less than 1% of the target and indicating minimal real‑world impact on fuel consumption.

Daily PT trips total 1.24 M, roughly 14% below the pre‑pandemic average of 1.43 M. The ridership component of the MF‑Index (72.7) shows modest recovery, but further incentives are needed to close the gap.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction sectors report mobility scores of 85‑95 and WFH rates under 15%, exposing the economy to congestion, higher fuel demand and potential productivity losses if traffic conditions worsen.

WFH adoption is uneven: public & GLC employees enjoy 60% WFH, whereas high‑risk private sectors are below 15%. This disparity limits the overall effectiveness of the remote‑work mandate and raises equity concerns.

Elevated fuel prices (RON95 RM4.42/L, diesel RM5.27/L) could encourage a shift to public transport or low‑emission modes, yet low actual fuel savings and high private‑sector mobility suggest the shift is not yet materialising.

recommendation: Introduce sector‑specific WFH targets – at least 30% for Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction by Q2 2027 – coupled with a modest PT fare subsidy for commuters in high‑mobility zones. Complement these measures with a fuel‑tax rebate for low‑emission vehicle purchases to accelerate modal shift and improve equity.
